intro: A martial arts school sign makes a claim. It names an art, and often a founder, a style or a headquarters far away. Behind the sign stand older institutions: a Japanese scroll listing headmasters since the 1400s, a Tokyo registry of dan ranks begun in 1883, a Seoul headquarters opened in 1972, or a Brazilian family academy opened in Rio de Janeiro in 1925.

In this unit you will study who has the power to name an art and grant its rank. You will compare teachers, federations, governments and courts. You will also compare village festivals, such as Kırkpınar in Edirne and Naadam in Mongolia, with the Olympic Games, where one international rule book sets the weight classes and the clock.

By the end, you will be able to explain what a certificate promises and who stands behind it. You will be able to name the laws and bodies that decide disputes over names. You will also be able to weigh what an art gains and gives up when it trades local custom for a world stage.
bigQuestion: Who has the authority to name a martial art, grant its ranks and write its rules?

title: Who Hangs the Sign

chapters.title: Lineage and a Certificate
chapters.bigQuestion: When two schools claim the same art, who has the power to say which certificate counts?

story.title: Two Frames by the Door
story.kicker: A new student notices that two rank papers on one wall trace back to two different founders.
paragraphs: A tenth grader named Dania walks into a taekwondo school in a small Illinois strip mall. She has come to sign up for Saturday classes. While the owner finds a form, Dania looks at the wall by the front desk. Two framed certificates hang side by side, each with the owner's name in large letters.

The first certificate is printed in Korean and English. At the top it says Kukkiwon, with an address in Seoul. A long registration number runs along the bottom edge. The second certificate carries a different seal and a small photo of an older man in a white uniform. Under the photo is the name Choi Hong-hi.

Dania asks why there are two. The owner laughs and says the art split into two big families in the 1960s and 1970s. One family looks to the Kukkiwon, opened in Seoul in 1972. The other looks to the International Taekwon-Do Federation, which General Choi founded in 1966. The owner says he trained under teachers from both.

Dania thinks of a family tree, where every person has two grandfathers. Each certificate is a claim about where the owner's knowledge came from. Each also names an institution that promises to stand behind that claim. She wonders which one a tournament, a college club or a court would believe.
story.think: What does a rank certificate prove, and whose promise stands behind it?

sections.title: Older Ways to Pass On an Art

lessons.title: Scrolls and Licenses
lessons.mainIdea: Older Japanese martial schools passed on authority through written licenses from a teacher, not through a national rank system.
reading: Japanese historians use the word *koryū*, meaning old-style school, for martial traditions founded before the Meiji era began in 1868. One well-known example is Tenshin Shōden Katori Shintō-ryū. The school traditionally dates its founding to the 1400s in what is now Chiba Prefecture. Each koryū keeps a list of its past headmasters, running back to a founder.

Many koryū gave students written licenses at set stages of study. The highest was often called *menkyo kaiden*, the license of complete transmission. It said the holder had received the whole curriculum of that school. Licenses were often written by hand on a *makimono*, a rolled paper scroll. The scroll named the founder and each teacher in the chain down to the student.

This system tied authority to a person, not to an office in a capital city. A license from one headmaster meant nothing inside a rival school. Arts outside the martial world worked the same way. Japanese tea schools and flower-arranging schools used a head-of-house system called iemoto, where one family controlled the right to teach and to grant licenses.

words.d: an old-style Japanese martial school founded before the Meiji era began in 1868
the license of complete transmission, the highest license in many old Japanese schools
a rolled paper scroll; many old licenses were written on one
a Japanese head-of-house system in which one family controls teaching and licenses

lessons.title: Numbered Ranks at the Kodokan
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō Jigorō gave judo numbered dan ranks in the 1880s, tying rank to an institution that keeps records.
reading: Kanō Jigorō opened the Kodokan in 1882 in a small space at Eishō-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. He had studied older jūjutsu schools that used licenses. For his new judo, he chose a different tool. In 1883 he named his first two *shodan*, or first-degree ranks: Saigō Shirō and Tomita Tsunejirō.

The word *dan* means step or grade. Players of the board game go had used dan grades in Japan since the 1600s. Kanō borrowed that idea of numbered steps. A student could rise from first dan upward, and each promotion was written in the Kodokan's records. Kyū grades, counted downward, were later used for students below first dan.

The change moved authority from a single teacher's scroll to an institution with a *registry*, a list kept over time. A Kodokan rank could be checked in Tokyo decades later. The Kodokan still issues and records dan grades today. Only a small number of people have ever received its tenth dan, the highest grade it has awarded.

words.d: a numbered step or grade of rank, used first in the game of go and later in judo
first-degree rank, the first dan
an official list kept over time, such as a record of every rank an institution has awarded

lessons.title: A National Office for Titles
lessons.mainIdea: Imperial Japan's Dai Nippon Butokukai granted martial titles from 1895 until the occupation dissolved it after 1945.
reading: In 1895 a group founded the *Dai Nippon Butokukai*, or Greater Japan Martial Virtue Association, in Kyoto. It had imperial patronage and branches across Japan. In 1899 it opened the Butokuden, a large training hall in Kyoto. Each year it held gatherings where teachers of many arts demonstrated before judges.

The Butokukai did something no single school could do. It granted national teaching titles across many arts, including kendo, judo and archery. Early in the 1900s it began awarding titles such as *hanshi* and kyōshi to senior teachers. Karate teachers from Okinawa later sought these titles too. A Butokukai title told the public that a national body had approved the holder.

The Butokukai grew closely tied to the wartime state in the 1930s and 1940s. After Japan's defeat in 1945, the Allied occupation saw it as part of that militarism. The association was dissolved in 1946. Its end showed that a body that grants titles depends on the government and laws around it.

words.d: Greater Japan Martial Virtue Association, founded in Kyoto in 1895 and dissolved in 1946
a senior teaching title granted by the Butokukai and later by other Japanese bodies
support and protection from a powerful person or family, such as an emperor

lessons.title: Funakoshi and the Shōtōkan Name
lessons.mainIdea: Funakoshi Gichin brought Okinawan karate to Tokyo in 1922, and his students later named a style after his dojo.
reading: Funakoshi Gichin was born in 1868 in Shuri, on Okinawa, the center of the old Ryukyu Kingdom. Japan had annexed the kingdom as Okinawa Prefecture in 1879. In 1922 Funakoshi gave a karate demonstration in Tokyo at an exhibition sponsored by the Ministry of Education. He stayed in Tokyo and taught in university clubs.

To fit Tokyo's martial world, Funakoshi borrowed judo's dan ranks and white uniforms. He also published books in Japanese, starting in 1922. He signed his poems with the pen name Shōtō, meaning pine waves. In 1939 his supporters opened a dojo in Tokyo and hung a sign reading *Shōtōkan*, the hall of Shōtō. United States bombing destroyed the building in 1945.

Funakoshi mostly called what he taught simply karate-dō. His students began using the name of the lost hall as the name of a *style*, a school of karate with its own lineage and forms. The sign on one building became a claim carried by clubs around the world. A style name tells people which teacher a school says it descends from.

words.d: the hall of Shōtō, Funakoshi Gichin's Tokyo dojo, opened in 1939; later the name of a karate style
a school of an art with its own lineage, forms and name
to take over a territory and make it part of another country

lessons.title: One Teacher, Several Associations
lessons.mainIdea: After Funakoshi died in 1957, groups of his students formed rival associations, and a later split went to Japanese courts.
reading: In 1949 some of Funakoshi's students founded the *Japan Karate Association*, or JKA. In 1957 Japan's Ministry of Education recognized it as a legal corporation. Funakoshi died the same year, in April 1957. Another group of his older students kept their own association, the Shotokai. Both said they carried Funakoshi's teaching forward.

The JKA trained full-time instructors and sent many abroad in the 1960s. They opened clubs in Europe, the Americas and Africa. Each instructor gave rank certificates stamped with the JKA name. Nakayama Masatoshi served as the JKA's chief instructor for decades. In this way, one Tokyo association issued rank to students on several continents.

Nakayama died in 1987. Soon after, JKA leaders split into rival groups. Each side claimed to be the true JKA, and the dispute went to Japanese courts in the 1990s. Some instructors left and formed new associations with new names. A student's certificate now depended on which group the teacher had joined.

words.d: the JKA, a karate body founded in Tokyo in 1949 by students of Funakoshi Gichin
an organized group with members, leaders and rules, often able to issue rank
an organization recognized by law as able to own property, sign contracts and go to court

lessons.title: From Maeda to the Gracies
lessons.mainIdea: Brazilian jiu-jitsu grew from judo brought to Brazil by Maeda Mitsuyo, and the Gracie family made its name part of the art.
reading: Maeda Mitsuyo was a Kodokan judo student born in 1878. He left Japan in 1904 and traveled through the United States, Europe and Latin America, often in public contests. In 1914 he reached Brazil. He settled in Belém, a port city in the state of Pará, near the mouth of the Amazon River. He died there in 1941.

According to the Gracie family's account, Carlos Gracie learned from Maeda in Belém as a teenager. Carlos and his brothers later taught in Rio de Janeiro, where the family opened an academy in 1925. Historians note that Maeda also taught others in Belém, such as Luiz França. The family story is one important *lineage* claim among several.

The Gracie brothers, especially Carlos and Hélio, made their family name part of the art's identity. In 1978 Hélio's son Rorion Gracie moved to Southern California to teach. In 1993 he helped create the Ultimate Fighting Championship, whose first event was held in Denver. His brother Royce won it, and interest in *Brazilian jiu-jitsu* spread fast.

words.d: a line of teachers and students traced back through time to a founder or source
a grappling art that grew in Brazil from judo taught by Maeda Mitsuyo and others
a story of events told by a person or group, which historians compare with other evidence

lessons.title: A Headquarters in Seoul
lessons.mainIdea: The Kukkiwon, opened in Seoul in 1972, issues taekwondo dan certificates that are registered and recognized worldwide.
reading: After Korea's liberation from Japanese rule in 1945, several training halls called *kwan* opened in Seoul. Among them were the Chung Do Kwan, the Moo Duk Kwan and the Jido Kwan. Each had its own founder and its own ranks. In the 1950s and 1960s, Korean leaders worked to unite the kwan under one name, taekwondo.

The South Korean government backed a central headquarters. The *Kukkiwon* opened in Seoul on November 30, 1972. In 1973 the World Taekwondo Federation was founded there to run international competition. It changed its name to World Taekwondo in 2017. The Kukkiwon kept the job of setting forms and granting dan rank.

A Kukkiwon certificate carries a registration number that can be checked against its records. Students under fifteen receive a *poom* rank instead of a dan. Many national federations in the World Taekwondo family recognize Kukkiwon rank for their black belts. That is why many schools abroad hang a Kukkiwon certificate by the door.

words.d: a Korean training hall or school; several kwan opened in Seoul after 1945
the taekwondo headquarters in Seoul, opened in 1972, which grants dan and poom rank
a Kukkiwon rank for students under fifteen, matched to dan rank

lessons.title: What a Governing Body Keeps
lessons.mainIdea: A governing body keeps rules, records and membership lists, which gives its certificates weight beyond one school.
reading: A *governing body* is an organization that sets rules for a sport and decides who may compete. In the United States, the Amateur Sports Act of 1978 set up one national governing body for each Olympic sport. It was renamed the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act in 1998. USA Judo, USA Taekwondo and USA Wrestling each hold that role for their sports.

A governing body keeps things a single teacher cannot. It keeps a membership list, a rule book, a list of certified referees and a registry of rank. Its tournaments decide who goes to national and world championships. A rank from it can be checked years later, even after a local school closes.

Brazilian jiu-jitsu built its own body. The International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation, or IBJJF, was founded in 2002 by Carlos Gracie Jr. It registers black belts and sets minimum ages for adult belts. Under its rules, a person must be at least nineteen to receive a black belt. A school that wants its students in IBJJF events follows those rules.

words.d: an organization that sets rules for a sport and decides who may compete
a 1978 U.S. law that set up one national governing body for each Olympic sport
the youngest age at which a rule allows a person to hold a rank or enter an event

lessons.title: Two Taekwondo Families
lessons.mainIdea: Choi Hong-hi's International Taekwon-Do Federation grew apart from the Kukkiwon, so taekwondo has two major lines of rank.
reading: Choi Hong-hi was a South Korean army general who taught martial arts to soldiers in the 1950s. He was part of the group that chose the name taekwondo in 1955. In 1966 he founded the *International Taekwon-Do Federation*, or ITF, in Seoul. He wrote its forms and its rules.

Choi fell out with South Korea's government in the early 1970s. In 1972 he moved the ITF's headquarters to Toronto, Canada. He later brought ITF teachers to North Korea. Meanwhile, the Kukkiwon and the World Taekwondo Federation grew in Seoul with state support. Taekwondo became an Olympic demonstration sport in 1988, and a full medal sport in 2000 under World Taekwondo rules.

Choi died in 2002 in Pyongyang. After his death, the ITF split into several groups, each with its own president and certificates. So a taekwondo *black belt* can come from the Kukkiwon line or from one of several ITF lines. The forms, the scoring rules and the names on the certificates differ between the families.

words.d: the ITF, founded in Seoul in 1966 by Choi Hong-hi and later moved to Toronto
the belt worn by holders of first dan and above in many modern martial arts
a sport shown at the Olympic Games without counting in the official medal table

lessons.title: A Family Name as a Mark
lessons.mainIdea: Trademark law lets a business own a name for its services, which turned the Gracie family name into a legal question.
reading: A *trademark* is a word, name or symbol that tells buyers who is selling a product or service. In the United States, the Lanham Act of 1946 is the main federal trademark law. A business can register a mark with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. The owner can then sue others who use the mark in a way that confuses buyers.

After moving to California, Rorion Gracie registered the name Gracie Jiu-Jitsu as a trademark. But the Gracie family was large, and many relatives taught under their own name. In the 1990s, family members took disputes over the name to U.S. federal courts. The question was whether one branch could own the family name as a mark for teaching.

The Gracie cases show a clash between two kinds of authority. Lineage says a name belongs to everyone taught in a line. Trademark law says a name belongs to whoever registers and uses it in trade. A *federal court* decides these cases under statutes, not under the customs of a school.

words.d: a word, name or symbol that shows who sells a product or service; it can be registered and protected by law
the main U.S. federal trademark law, passed in 1946
a U.S. national court that decides cases under federal laws such as the Lanham Act

look.prompt: Which argument rests on lineage, and which rests on trademark law? Which one would a federal court look at first?

lessons.title: Generic Words and Protected Names
lessons.mainIdea: Common art names cannot be owned, but some names, such as Olympic and Shaolin, are protected by law or registration.
reading: Trademark law does not let anyone own a *generic term*, the everyday name for a kind of thing. Words like karate, judo and taekwondo name whole arts. Any school may put them on its sign. A school can only register its own distinct name, such as a family name joined to a style.

Some names get special protection. The Amateur Sports Act gives the U.S. Olympic Committee the exclusive right to use the word Olympic in the United States. In 1987 the U.S. Supreme Court upheld that right in San Francisco Arts and Athletics v. United States Olympic Committee. A group had planned to call its event the Gay Olympic Games and was stopped.

Temples can register names too. Since the late 1990s, the Shaolin Temple in Dengfeng, Henan Province, has registered its name as a trademark in China and many other countries. The temple is linked in legend to Bodhidharma and to the start of Chinese boxing, stories historians treat as legend. Today its *registration* lets it act in court over who may use the name.

story.title: Two Kinds of Güreş
story.kicker: A family watches wrestling in Edirne and then in Paris a few weeks later, and the same word names two different worlds.
paragraphs: In the summer of 2024, a family from Istanbul sits in the stands at Sarayiçi, a meadow beside the river in Edirne, Turkey. Hundreds of wrestlers in heavy leather trousers wait their turn. Each is shining with olive oil. Drummers and players of the zurna, a loud reed pipe, play as pairs are called onto the field.

This is Kırkpınar, the oil wrestling festival that Edirne holds every summer. The Turkish word for wrestling is güreş. Here the wrestlers are grouped by age and experience, and many bouts run at once on the grass. The grand winner is named başpehlivan, or chief wrestler, and receives a golden belt.

A few weeks later the same family watches the Paris Olympic Games on television. The wrestling is held indoors at the Champ-de-Mars Arena, on a round mat of set size. Each bout has two periods of three minutes. Wrestlers weigh in the morning of competition and compete in fixed weight classes. The Turkish broadcast still calls it güreş.

The grandmother points out that both events use one word. Yet one answers to a city, a festival and centuries of local custom. The other answers to United World Wrestling and the International Olympic Committee. The family wonders what each one had to give up to become what it is.
story.think: If two events share a name but answer to different institutions, are they the same art?

lessons.title: Kırkpınar in Edirne
lessons.mainIdea: Kırkpınar oil wrestling is run by the city of Edirne under local custom, not by an Olympic federation.
reading: *Kırkpınar* is held each summer in Edirne, a city in northwestern Turkey near the borders with Greece and Bulgaria. Its organizers trace the festival to the 1300s, in the early Ottoman period. That founding date rests on tradition and a legend about forty soldiers, not on a record from the time. Documents show the festival well established by the Ottoman centuries that followed.

Wrestlers wear the *kispet*, heavy trousers made of water buffalo or calf leather. They coat themselves with olive oil before bouts. Wrestlers are grouped by age and experience rather than by body weight on a scale. The top class competes for the title of başpehlivan and a golden belt.

The festival has its own officials and ceremonies. An announcer called the cazgır introduces wrestlers in rhymed verse. The Edirne city government runs the event. In 2010 UNESCO added the Kırkpınar oil wrestling festival to its Representative List of the *Intangible Cultural Heritage* of Humanity.

lessons.title: Naadam and Mongolian Wrestling
lessons.mainIdea: Mongolian wrestling at the Naadam festival keeps its own titles and customs, including traditionally having no weight classes.
reading: *Naadam* is Mongolia's national summer festival, held each year in July. Its three main contests are wrestling, horse racing and archery, often called the three games of men. The national Naadam in Ulaanbaatar opens on July 11, the date of the 1921 revolution. Towns and districts across the country hold their own Naadam as well.

Mongolian wrestling, called bökh, traditionally has no weight classes. A small wrestler may meet a very large one. Wrestlers wear the zodog, a short jacket open across the chest, and the shuudag, tight briefs. A popular story says the jacket is open because a woman once entered in disguise and won. That tale is a legend, not a dated record.

Winners earn state titles named after strong animals, such as arslan, meaning lion. The highest title is avarga, often translated as titan. Before and after bouts, wrestlers perform an eagle dance, described by many Mongolians as a show of honor. In 2010 UNESCO listed Naadam as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Mongolian wrestling, traditionally held with no weight classes

lessons.title: Schwingen in the Sawdust
lessons.mainIdea: Swiss schwingen answers to a national wrestling association and a festival held every three years, with a live bull as a prize.
reading: Schwingen is a style of wrestling from the Swiss Alps and the lands around them. Bouts take place in a ring of sawdust. Each wrestler wears short canvas trousers pulled over regular clothes. Wrestlers traditionally shake hands before a bout, and the winner brushes sawdust from the loser's back after it.

The Unspunnen festival near Interlaken, first held in 1805, helped make schwingen a national symbol. The Federal Wrestling Association, or Eidgenössischer Schwingerverband, was founded in 1895. It runs the *Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival*, held every three years. Hundreds of thousands of people visit the festival grounds.

Schwingen has no weight classes. The overall winner is named Schwingerkönig, or king of the schwingers. The main prize is a live bull, a reminder of the art's farming roots. Schwingen is not part of the Olympic Games. Its rules answer to a Swiss association, not to an international federation.

lessons.title: Judo Comes to Tokyo, 1964
lessons.mainIdea: Judo joined the Olympic Games at Tokyo in 1964 with weight classes, and a Dutch champion's win changed who owned the sport.
reading: The *International Judo Federation*, or IJF, was founded in 1951. Its members were national judo bodies from several countries. When Tokyo won the 1964 Olympic Games, Japan pushed to add judo. The Nippon Budokan hall was built in Tokyo for the judo events. Judo became the first Asian martial art on the Olympic program.

Kodokan judo had no weight classes in its early decades. A small player might face a large one. For Tokyo 1964, organizers set up four divisions: lightweight, middleweight, heavyweight and an open class for all sizes. This *weight class* system followed Western wrestling and boxing, which already used them.

Japanese players won three of the four events. In the open class, Anton Geesink of the Netherlands defeated Kaminaga Akio before a crowd at the Budokan. Many in Japan felt shock. Geesink's win showed that judo was now a world sport, and that its rules would be set by an international federation, not by Tokyo alone.

lessons.title: A Blue Jacket and a Clock
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic judo changed its uniforms and timing so audiences could follow it, which some traditional teachers opposed.
reading: Judo left the program at Mexico City in 1968 and returned at Munich in 1972. It has been at every Summer Games since. Women's judo appeared as a demonstration event at Seoul in 1988. It became a full medal sport at Barcelona in 1992. Today men and women each have seven Olympic weight classes.

In the 1990s the IJF approved a blue *judogi*, the judo uniform, for one athlete in each match. The other athlete wears white. Blue jackets were first used at the Olympics in Sydney in 2000. Anton Geesink had argued for them so referees, judges and TV viewers could tell the two players apart. The Kodokan and many Japanese teachers opposed the change, preferring the white judogi alone.

The IJF also controls the clock and the cloth. Since 2017, regular time for Olympic judo bouts has been four minutes for both men and women. If the score is tied, a *golden score* period continues until someone scores. The IJF also approves which uniforms may be worn at its events, with labels showing they meet its rules.

lessons.title: Taekwondo and Electronic Scoring
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic taekwondo adopted electronic scoring vests to answer judging disputes, reshaping the sport around a sensor.
reading: Taekwondo appeared as a demonstration sport at the 1988 Seoul Olympics and again at Barcelona in 1992. It became a full medal sport at Sydney in 2000. The Olympic program has four weight classes for men and four for women, fewer than the eight each at world championships. So some athletes must move up or down a class to reach the Games.

Early Olympic taekwondo relied on corner judges pressing buttons to award points. Disputed decisions caused protests, including at the 2008 Beijing Games. World Taekwondo, then named the World Taekwondo Federation, responded with electronic scoring. At the London Olympics in 2012, athletes wore a *protector and scoring system*, or PSS, with sensors in the vest and foot socks.

Instant video replay was also added so coaches could challenge calls. These tools made scoring more open to review. They also changed what counted as a scoring contact. The sport on the Olympic mat now answers to a rule book and a sensor. A local school's sparring rules, set by its own teachers, answer to no such *technology*.

lessons.title: Two Styles in the Rule Book
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic wrestling uses two styles, Greco-Roman and freestyle, each shaped by nineteenth- and twentieth-century rule makers.
reading: Wrestling was on the program of the ancient Olympic Games, starting in 708 BCE by tradition. The modern Games of 1896 in Athens held one wrestling event. It followed a style developed in nineteenth-century France and later called *Greco-Roman*. Despite the name, it was a modern style, not a copy of ancient Greek wrestling. Its rules ban holds below the waist.

Freestyle wrestling grew from catch-as-catch-can wrestling in Britain and the United States. It first appeared at the Olympics in St. Louis in 1904, where every entrant was American. The international federation now called United World Wrestling was founded in 1912. It was long known by its French initials, FILA, and took its current name in 2014.

Women's freestyle wrestling joined the Olympics at Athens in 2004. In February 2013, the IOC's executive board recommended dropping wrestling from future Games. Wrestling bodies changed leaders and rules, and in September 2013 the IOC voted to keep the sport. The episode showed that even the oldest Olympic sport stays only as long as the IOC agrees.

lessons.title: Karate's Single Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Karate was an Olympic sport only at Tokyo 2020, and fitting it in meant merging classes and choosing one federation's rules.
reading: Karate began on Okinawa and spread to mainland Japan in the 1920s. By the late 1900s, it had many styles and many associations. The World Union of Karate-do Organizations formed in 1970 to run world championships. It later became the *World Karate Federation*, or WKF, which the IOC recognized as karate's international federation.

Tokyo won the 2020 Games, and karate was added as a host-city sport. Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Games were held in 2021. Karate took place at the Nippon Budokan. There were two disciplines: *kata*, solo forms judged by a panel, and kumite, scored bouts. Olympic kumite had three weight classes per sex, merged from the five used at WKF world championships.

Karate was not kept for Paris 2024 or Los Angeles 2028. Some karate teachers said the Olympic format favored one federation's rules over the many styles. Others said the Games brought karate new attention. Under IOC rules, a host city may propose extra sports, so an art's Olympic place can depend on who hosts.

a set series of karate movements performed alone and judged by a panel in competition

lessons.title: Wushu Outside the Rings
lessons.mainIdea: China built competition wushu as a state sport with set routines, and it has sought Olympic status without gaining it.
reading: China has many local martial traditions, each tied to a region, a family or a village. After 1949, the People's Republic of China set up a state sports system. In the 1950s its sports officials created standard *wushu* routines for competition. Judges scored routines for form and difficulty, much like gymnastics.

The International Wushu Federation, or IWUF, was founded in 1990. Competition wushu has two main parts. Taolu are set routines, with or without weapons. Sanda, also called sanshou, is scored full-contact bouts. Wushu has been on the Asian Games program since Beijing hosted in 1990.

China asked to add wushu to the 2008 Beijing Olympics. The IOC did not make it a medal sport. Instead, it allowed a separate Beijing 2008 Wushu Tournament during the Games. Many older family and village styles do not fit either taolu or sanda. So the *state* version of wushu and the local styles answer to different institutions.

lessons.title: Muay Thai: Stadiums and Temple Fairs
lessons.mainIdea: Muay Thai moved from temple fairs to Bangkok stadiums with gloves and rings, then built an amateur federation seeking Olympic status.
reading: For centuries, boxing bouts in Siam, now Thailand, took place at temple fairs and festivals. Fighters wrapped their hands in rope or cloth. In the 1920s and 1930s, Bangkok rings began requiring gloves and set rounds, borrowed from Western boxing. Rajadamnern Stadium opened in 1945. Lumpinee Stadium, run by the Royal Thai Army, opened in 1956.

Before a bout, fighters perform the *wai khru*, a ritual of respect to teachers, and a dance called ram muay. Many wear a headband called the mongkhon, which the fighter's teacher places and removes. Musicians play a pipe and drums during the bout. These customs stayed in the stadium even as the rules changed.

In 1993 the International Federation of Muaythai Associations, or *IFMA*, was founded to run amateur competition. Amateur rules add protective gear and shorter bouts. The IOC gave IFMA provisional recognition in 2016 and full recognition in 2021. Recognition is a step toward the Olympic program, but it does not guarantee a place at the Games.

lessons.title: The IOC's Power to Recognize
lessons.mainIdea: The IOC recognizes one international federation per sport, and it can withdraw that recognition, as it did with boxing in 2023.
reading: The *Olympic Charter* is the IOC's founding rule book. It says the IOC recognizes international federations to govern their sports at the world level. Normally the IOC recognizes one federation for each sport. That federation writes the competition rules and runs qualifying events for the Games.

Boxing has been on the Olympic program since St. Louis in 1904, except in 1912. For decades, its federation was known as AIBA, later renamed the International Boxing Association, or IBA. The IOC raised concerns about its judging, finances and leadership. It suspended the federation in 2019 and ran the boxing events itself at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024.

In June 2023 the IOC withdrew its *recognition* of the IBA altogether. A new body, World Boxing, was founded in 2023. The IOC recognized World Boxing in 2025 and kept boxing on the program for Los Angeles 2028. A sport's Olympic place depends on its federation keeping the IOC's trust.

words.d: the IOC's founding rule book, which sets out how the Olympic movement is governed
formal approval by a higher body, such as the IOC approving a federation
a world body that governs one sport and writes its competition rules

lessons.title: UNESCO and a Different Kind of Value
lessons.mainIdea: UNESCO's heritage lists value martial traditions as living culture, which is a different kind of recognition from the Olympic path.
reading: In 2003 UNESCO adopted the Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, often called the *Intangible Heritage Convention*. It asks countries to protect living customs, such as music, crafts, festivals and games. Countries nominate traditions for UNESCO's lists. The lists do not set rules for competition. They honor a practice's place in the life of a community.

Several martial traditions are on the lists. The Korean art of taekkyeon was listed in 2011. The capoeira circle of Brazil, the roda, was listed in 2014. In 2018, North and South Korea jointly nominated ssireum, Korean wrestling, the first such joint listing by the two countries. In 2019 UNESCO listed pencak silat from Indonesia and silat from Malaysia as separate entries.

Olympic recognition and UNESCO listing reward different things. The Olympic path rewards a single international rule book, weight classes and a clock. The UNESCO path rewards *safeguarding*, keeping a practice alive with its music, clothing and local meanings. An art can pursue both, but each answers to a different institution with different goals.
